title.en: The King of Ulster's Son Slays Dolar Durba
title.zh: 阿爾斯特王子誅殺多拉·杜爾巴

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: A twelve-year-old prince of Ulster, shut up by a father who thinks his bones too soft, escapes with twelve foster-brothers to join Finn at the White Strand. Conan mocks him; the invaders laugh when Finn's side sends a lad against their champion Dolar Durba — and in the mock they die, for the boy wounds Dolar again and again, grapples him when shields break, and the tide drowns them both locked together, Dolar beneath him.
summary.zh: 十二歲的阿爾斯特王子被父親以「骨骼尚軟」為由禁閉，卻攜十二名奶兄弟逃往白沙灘投奔芬恩。科南嘲弄他；當芬恩一方派出一少年迎戰敵方最強戰士多拉·杜爾巴時，敵軍大笑——然而大笑者皆亡：少年連創多拉，盾劍俱碎後相搏扭打，潮水將二人相鎖溺斃，多拉居其下。

sensitivity.note: The boy-hero episode is a Fenian stock type (compare Cuchulain's first exploits); the mutual drowning in a death-grip is the fixed 'sole to sole' death-motif of this cycle. Pin symbolic at the White Strand battle site.

passages.text: News of the great battle reached to the court of the King of Ulster, and the king's son, that was only twelve years of age and the comeliest of all the young men of Ireland, said to his father: "Let me go to help Finn, son of Cumhal, and his men." "You are not old enough, or strong enough, boy; your bones are too soft." When the boy went on asking, his father shut him up in some close place, and put twelve young men, his foster-brothers, in charge of him. "It is through courage and daring my father won a great name for himself in his young youth, and why does he keep me from winning a name for myself?" The boy talked on till he got round them all, and when the king was asleep they went into the house where the arms were kept, and every lad brought away a shield and a sword and a helmet and two spears and two greyhound whelps, and they went through Connacht of many tribes and into Ciarraighe, and so on to the White Strand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came there Dolar Durba was on the strand, boasting before the men of Ireland. "You are not a grown man," said Conan; "and neither yourself or your comrades are fit to face any fighting man at all." "I never saw the Fianna of Ireland till this day, but I know well that you are Conan Maol, that never says a good word of any man; and you will see now if I am in dread of that man on the strand, or of any man in the world, for I will go out against him by myself." But it was then Conan told him Dolar Durba was just after killing his twelve comrades.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Great anger came on him, and he rushed down to the strand; and all the armies of the strangers gave a great shout of laughter, for they thought all Finn's men had been made an end of. When the boy heard that his courage grew the greater, and he fell on Dolar Durba and gave him many wounds before he knew he was attacked at all. They fought till their shields and their swords were broken in pieces, and then they grappled together and wrestled till the tide went over them and drowned them both; and when the ebb-tide came on the morrow, the two bodies were found cold and quiet, each one held fast by the other, but Dolar Durba was beneath the king's son, so they knew it was the young lad had got the victory.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fall of the King of Lochlann and His Sons
title.zh: 洛赫蘭王與三子之傾覆

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. X, eBook #14465

summary.en: The royal house of Lochlann falls one after another on the strand: Forne falls to Oisin heartened by Fergus's praise, Tocha to Lugaidh's Son, Mongach of the Sea to Fidach of the Bretons in a mutual death of flail and sword. Last comes Caisel of the Feathers with the shield of the Fomor's smith that blazes even under the sea and burns men like oak-splinters — until Druimderg casts the Red-Socketed spear into his laughing mouth and the flame of the shield dies.
summary.zh: 洛赫蘭王室在白沙灘相繼傾覆：弗恩經費爾古斯讚美後的歐辛誅殺；托哈死於盧蓋德之子；海上之蒙古赫與布列塔尼之菲達赫同歸於盡。最後是持弗莫爾鐵匠神盾的羽翎王凱塞爾——盾焰入水不熄，焚人如燒橡柴——直到德魯姆德格擲出紅臼矛，正中其張口大笑之處，盾焰方熄。

sensitivity.note: The fire-shield of the Fomor's smith is a magical-weapon set-piece of the Fenian marvel repertoire; the mocking laugh that leaves only the mouth unarmoured is a fixed death-motif (compare Balor's eye, Siegfried's back). Pin symbolic at the strand.

passages.text: "I swear by the oath of my people," said the King of Lochlann, "if any man of the armies goes out against the Fianna before myself and my three sons, we will not go at all, for we would not get the satisfaction we are used to, unless our swords get their fill of blood." "I will go out against them alone," said Forne, the youngest son, with a red-edged sword in each of his hands, and he made the strand narrow with the bodies of the young men of the Fianna.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Oisin gave out a great shout against him: "Stop here with me, king's son, until I fight with you for the Fianna." It seemed for a while that the battle was going against Oisin, and Fergus of the True Lips said to him: "There is great shame on the Fianna, Oisin, seeing you so low in this fight; and there is many a horseman from the daughters of the kings and princes of Ireland looking at you now." Great courage rose in Oisin then, and he drove his spear through the body of Forne. And Tocha, the second son, went on shore to avenge his brother, till Lugaidh's Son turned against him, and made a stroke that cut through the foreigner's sword, and then another that cut his heart in two halves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: The third son, Mongach of the Sea, went on shore with a strong iron flail in his hand having seven balls of pure iron on it, and fifty iron chains, and fifty apples on every chain, and fifty deadly thorns on every apple. Fidach, son of the King of the Bretons, went out against him, and leaped aside from the flail and cut off his two hands at the joint, and made a blow at his middle that cut him into two halves; but as Mongach fell, an apple of the flail went into Fidach's comely mouth and through his brain, and it was foot to foot those two fell, and lip to lip.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: And the next that came was the King of Lochlann himself, Caisel of the Feathers, and the shield that was made for him by the smith of the Fomor had red flames coming from it; and if it was put under the sea itself, not one of its flames would stop blazing; and the flames he sent from his shield went through the bodies of men till they blazed up like a splinter of oak that had hung a year in the smoke of a chimney. Then Druimderg, grandson of the Head of the Fianna of Ulster, took the deadly spear, the Croderg, the Red-Socketed, that came down from one to another of the sons of Rudraighe, and looked at the King of Lochlann, and he could see no part of him without armour but his mouth that was opened wide, laughing at the Fianna; and he made a cast with the Croderg that hit him in the open mouth, and he fell, and his shield fell along with its master, and its flame went out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. X; not verbatim.

title.en: Labran's Eagle Flight for the Fated Weapons
title.zh: 拉布蘭化身蒼鷹尋取宿命兵器

region.en: Dun of the King of the Country of the Fair Men (symbolic pin, western sea)
region.zh: 俊美者之國王的堡壘（象徵定位，西海）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. XI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Tadg's wife recalls a birth-night prophecy: the smith of the Fomor made a shield and a sword for Daire Donn, King of the World, and no other arms will ever redden on him — and they lie with the King of the Country of the Fair Men, locked room by room behind seven locks. Labran flies there as a great eagle, borrows the weapons under a false love-errand, and nearly dies of the speed of his return; the wind-swift Aedh son of Aebinn carries them the last leg, and flashes of fire rise from the coverings as Finn takes them.
summary.zh: 塔格之妻憶及誕生夜之預言：弗莫爾鐵匠曾為大世界之王達爾·東鑄盾與劍，除此之外天下任何兵器均無法見血——如今七重鎖层层相扣，藏於俊美者之國王處。拉布蘭化身巨鷹飛往彼處，以假借之辭借得兵器，歸程急馳幾近衰竭；疾如風的艾德接力最後一程。芬恩揭開兵器之覆時，火光與致命之泡自其中升騰。

sensitivity.note: Fated weapons only able to kill a specific foe is a fixed Indo-European dragon-slayer motif (compare Sigurd, Mordred); the eagle-transformation flight is a shape-shifter errand of the Ulster-Tuatha interface. Symbolic pin; the Country of the Fair Men has no earthly coordinates.

passages.text: Fergus of the True Lips went through the length of Ireland till he came to the house of Tadg, son of Nuada, that was grandfather to Finn, and there was great grief on Muirne, Finn's mother, and on Labran of the Long Hand her brother. Tadg asked his wife who did she think would escape with their lives from the great fighting at the White Strand. "If all the living men of the world were on one side, Daire Donn, the King of the World, would put them all down, for there are no weapons in the world that will ever be reddened on him. And on the night he was born, the smith of the Fomor made a shield and a sword, and it is in the prophecy that he will fall by no other arms but those. And it is to the King of the Country of the Fair Men he gave them to keep, and it is with him they are now."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XI; not verbatim.

passages.text: They sent Labran looking for the weapons in the shape of a great eagle, and he went on from sea to sea till at noon on the morrow he came to the dun of the King of the Country of the Fair Men. There were seven rooms in the king's house that opened into one another, and on the first door was one lock, and on the second two locks, and so on to the door of the last room that had seven locks; and it was in that the sword and the shield that were made by the smith of the Fomor were kept.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XI; not verbatim.

passages.text: Labran asked the loan of them under the story of a wife of a champion of the Fianna that had given him her love, and they were brought out and given to him, with stalks of luck put with them. He went back across the seas again, and reached his father's dun between the crowing of the cock and the full light of day, and the weakness of death came on him; and it was Aedh, son of Aebinn, that was as quick as the wind over a plain, carried them the last leg to the White Strand. Finn took the coverings off them, and there rose from them flashes of fire and deadly bubbles, and not one of the Fianna could stay looking at them, but it put great courage into them to know they were with Finn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XI; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn Slays the King of the World

region.en: Finntraigh (White Strand), Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡科爾卡·迪夫尼白沙灘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. XII, eBook #14465

summary.en: On the last day the sea and hills and stones cry out the doom of the armies. Arcallach's axe turns on the King of the World's crown and sheds no blood; but when Finn meets him with the fated shield and sword, dread shakes the king and Finn cuts off his foot and then his head. The crown passes to Conmail, then to the woman-warrior Ogarmach — "it is in the prophecy the world will be owned by a woman" — until Finn cuts through the crown and her head; and the last two living men, Cael and Finnachta of the Teeth, drown one another hand to hand in the clear sea.
summary.zh: 末日之戰，海、山、石皆預鳴大軍之劫。阿卡拉克之斧劈王冠而不見血；然當芬恩持宿命之盾劍而來，恐懼令國王戰慄失色，芬恩斬其足而後斬其首。王冠先傳康麥爾，再傳女戰士奧加馬克——「預言曰：世界終將為女子所轄」——芬恩劈冠而斬其首。最後僅存的兩人，克爾與牙齒之芬納克特，在澄澈之海中手手相扼同溺而亡。

sensitivity.note: The doom-omens answered by the creatures of the high air are the Fenian Ragnarok-echo (sea chattering, stones crying, wind sobbing) — tagged 'world-renewal' as the cosmic reset after which the Fianna take charge of all Ireland. The crown-transfer sequence is a sacred-kingship motif.

passages.text: The King of the World came to the strand, and all that were left of the Fianna went out against them, and they were like thick woods meeting one another. Then the creatures of the high air answered to the battle, foretelling the destruction that would be done that day; and the sea chattered of the losses, and the waves gave heavy shouts keening them, and the water-beasts roared to one another, and the rough hills creaked with the danger of the battle, and the woods trembled mourning the heroes, and the grey stones cried out at their deeds, and the wind sobbed telling them, and the earth shook, foretelling the slaughter; and the cries of the grey armies put a blue cloak over the sun, and the clouds were dark.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the King of the World came towards Finn, and there was no one near him but Arcallach of the Black Axe, the first that ever brought a wide axe into Ireland. He made a terrible great blow of his axe at the king that went through his royal crown to the hair of his head, but did not take a drop of blood out of him, for the edge of the axe turned, and there went balls of fire over the plain from that blow; and the King of the World struck back at Arcallach and made two halves of him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Finn and the King of the World turned on one another, and when the king saw the sword and the shield in Finn's hand, he knew those were the weapons that were to bring him to his death, and great dread came on him, and his comeliness left him, and his fingers were shaking. They fought like two days of judgment for the possession of the world, and Finn gave great strokes that broke his shield and his sword, and cut off his left foot, and at the last he struck off his head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finnachta of the Teeth took up the royal crown and set it on the head of Conmail; and when Goll Garbh made an end of him, he brought it to where Ogarmach was, the daughter of the King of Greece: "Put on that crown, Ogarmach, as it is in the prophecy the world will be owned by a woman; and it will never be owned by any woman higher than yourself." She went to look for Finn, and though the woman-warrior fought for a long time, a blow from Finn reached to her at last and cut through the royal crown, and with a second blow he struck her head off. And when the two armies were fallen side by side there were none left fit to stand but Cael, son of Crimthan, and Finnachta of the Teeth; and Cael, mortally hurt, had Fergus carry him to the sea to swim after the foreigner, and when Finnachta stretched out his hand to him, Cael took hold of it at the wrist and gave a strong pull that brought him over the side, and their hands shut across one another's bodies, and they went down to the sand and the gravel of the clear sea.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XII; not verbatim.

title.en: Credhe's Lament and her Death for Cael
title.zh: 克蕾德之哀歌與其殉情

region.en: South of the White Strand, Corca Duibhne, Co. Kerry, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡白沙灘之南

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book III, ch. XIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Credhe searches the field of the dead for Cael. A crane above the marshes cannot shield both her nestlings from the fox; a stag nineteen days without grass or water laments the hind Finn killed — "it is no shame for me to die for grief after Cael." The waves put Cael's body back on the strand; she keens him in the famous harbour-lament, lays herself down beside him, dies of grief, and Caoilte raises the one stone over them. With the battle over, the great name of the armies of the World passes to the Fianna of Ireland for ever.
summary.zh: 克蕾德在屍橫遍野的戰場尋找克爾。澤上母鶴護不住兩隻雛鳥逃離狐狸；十九日不飲不食的牡鹿哀悼被芬恩射殺的母鹿——「我為克爾悲傷而死並不可恥」。海浪將克爾屍身推回沙灘，她為之唱起著名的港灣哀歌，隨即倒臥其側而死；卡爾特為二人立一石。大戰既畢，大世界大軍之名永歸愛爾蘭菲亞納。

sensitivity.note: The keening-lament (caoine) after battle is a real ritual genre embedded in narrative; the wife dying of grief beside her husband is a fixed death-motif ('dying of grief'). Post-war transfer of spoils and name marks the Fianna's world-guarantor role. Tag 'resurrection' here marks the ritual lament as renewal-of-the-dead practice, not belief claim.

passages.text: There came the women and the musicians and the physicians of the Fianna of Ireland to search out the kings and the princes of the Fianna and to bury them; and every one that might be healed was brought to a place of healing. Credhe, wife of Cael, went looking through the bodies for her comely comrade, crying as she went, and she saw a crane of the meadows and her two nestlings, and the cunning beast the fox watching the nestlings; and when the crane covered one of the birds to save it, he would make a rush at the other bird, the way she had to stretch herself out over the birds, and she would sooner have got her own death by the fox than her nestlings to be killed by him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It is no wonder I to have such love for my comely sweetheart," said Credhe, "and the bird in that distress about her nestlings." Then she heard a stag in Druim Ruighlenn above the harbour, that was making great lamentations for his hind, for they had been nine years together and Finn had killed the hind, and the stag was nineteen days without tasting grass or water. "It is no shame for me to die for grief after Cael, since the stag is shortening his life sorrowing after the hind."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: She met Fergus of the True Lips, and he had news: Cael and the last man left of the foreigners, Finnachta Fiaclach, were after drowning one another in the sea. And at that time the waves had put Cael back on the strand, and the women and the men of the Fianna raised him up and brought him to the south of the White Strand, and Credhe came to where he was and keened him: "The harbour roars, O the harbour roars, over the rushing race of the Headland of the Two Storms, the drowning of the hero of the Lake of the Two Dogs, that is what the waves are keening on the strand...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Since the son of Crimthann is drowned I will love no one after him for ever; many a king fell by his hand; his shield never cried out in the battle." After she had made that complaint, Credhe laid herself down beside Cael and died for grief after him, and they were put in the one grave, and it was Caoilte raised the stone over them. And the great name that was on the armies of the World went from them to the Fianna of Ireland; and they took the ships and the gold and the silver and all the spoils of the armies of the World, and from that time the Fianna had charge of the whole of Ireland until the time of their last battle, the sorrowful battle of Gabhra.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book III, ch. XIII; not verbatim.
